name: Coarse-to-Fine Retrieval and Re-scoring
question: Can a cheap pass narrow things down before a precise one?
summary: A multi-stage pattern, also called phased ranking or re-scoring. A cheap, approximate first layer (binary or compressed vectors, a coarse index) returns a generous candidate set. Each later layer is more precise and more expensive but sees far fewer items, ending with full-precision distances or a cross-encoder. Vector databases expose it as oversampling plus re-scoring.
useCases: Very large corpora with a strict latency budget
Quantized indexes that need a precise final score
Pipelines ending in an expensive re-ranker

items.detail: binary or PQ vectors over the whole corpus → top 1,000
fetch more candidates than needed at early layers
recall@k and latency after each layer

steps: Measure the cheap layer’s recall at several candidate counts
Size each layer so the next one rarely misses a true match
Keep full-precision vectors available for the final rescore
Track latency per layer to find the bottleneck
pitfalls: Anything the first layer misses is lost for good
Extra layers add latency and moving parts
The name means different things in different products, so check what yours does
remember: Wide and cheap first, narrow and exact last.
caption: Candidate counts are typical examples. Tune them against measured recall.

final = c3[np.argsort(-scores)]                # layer 4: ordered by relevance
exact = np.argsort(-(emb @ q))[:10]            # brute force, for evaluation only
recall = len(set(c3) & set(exact)) / 10        # measure on many sample queries

steps.title: Store three precisions
steps.text: Binary codes (128 B) and int8 (1 KB) sit in RAM; full float32 vectors (4 KB) stay on SSD. For one million vectors: 128 MB, 1 GB and 4.1 GB.

steps.title: Layer 1: Hamming scan
steps.text: XOR and popcount against every binary code is very cheap. Keep a generous 1,000 candidates, because anything dropped here is lost for good.

steps.title: Layer 2: int8 rescore
steps.text: Integer dot products on the 1,000 candidates restore most of the precision. Keep the top 100.

steps.title: Layer 3: exact rescore
steps.text: Fetch 100 full vectors from SSD and compute exact cosine similarity. Keep the top 10.

steps.title: Layer 4: cross-encoder
steps.text: A cross-encoder reads the query and each passage together and orders the last 10 by relevance rather than by vector distance.

steps.title: Measure recall per layer
steps.text: Compare with exact search on sample queries. Retention multiplies: 0.97 × 0.99 × 1.0 ≈ 0.96 of the true top 10 survive.

pros: Precise final scores within a tight latency budget
A cheap first layer makes huge corpora affordable in RAM
Each layer can be sized and measured separately
Expensive re-rankers run on only a few items
cons: First-layer misses can never be recovered
More stages add latency and moving parts
Full-precision vectors must be kept somewhere for rescoring
The name means different things in different products
avoidWhen: The corpus is small enough for exact or single-index search
The latency budget is too tight for even one extra stage

You design a four-layer search: binary codes, an optional int8 rescore, an exact rescore with full vectors from SSD, and an optional cross-encoder. library.name: Qdrant
library.what: Built-in scalar and binary quantization with oversampling and automatic rescoring on full vectors.

samples.code:
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models
client = QdrantClient("localhost", port=6333)

client.create_collection(
    "archive",
    vectors_config=models.VectorParams(size=1024, distance=models.Distance.COSINE),
    quantization_config=models.BinaryQuantization(
        binary=models.BinaryQuantizationConfig(always_ram=True)),   # layer 1 in RAM
)

hits = client.query_points(
    "archive", query=query_vec, limit=100,
    search_params=models.SearchParams(
        quantization=models.QuantizationSearchParams(
            rescore=True,          # layer 2: rescore with full vectors
            oversampling=10.0)),   # fetch 1,000 cheap candidates for 100 results
).points

top10 = cross_encoder_rerank(query_text, hits)[:10]           # layer 3

numericDrill.question: Layer 1 keeps 1,000 candidates with recall 0.97. Layer 2 keeps 100 and retains 0.99 of what it receives. Layer 3 keeps 10 and retains 0.95. End-to-end recall?
numericDrill.answer: 0.97 × 0.99 × 0.95 ≈ 0.91. Each layer's losses multiply, so the weakest early layer caps the whole pipeline.

interview.question: Why use several retrieval stages instead of one precise search?
interview.answer: Precise scoring is expensive per item. A cheap first stage shrinks millions of items to hundreds, so the costly stages run on few items and results stay near-precise within the latency budget.

interview.question: How do you size each stage?
interview.answer: Measure recall at several candidate counts per stage, pick the smallest count where the next stage rarely misses true matches, then check end-to-end recall and per-stage latency.

mistakes.fix: Oversample early; misses there are permanent

quiz.question: Layers keep 0.95, 0.99 and 1.0 of the true top 10. What is the end-to-end recall?
How many bytes does a binary code take for a 1,024-dimension vector?
quiz.explanation: One bit per dimension: 1,024 ÷ 8 = 128 bytes.

quiz.question: Which statements about layered search are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Candidates dropped by the first layer are lost for good
Each later layer is more precise per item
The final layer scans the whole corpus
quiz.explanation: Coarse to fine: cheap and wide first, precise and narrow last. The final layer sees only a handful of items.

quiz.question: 10 million 1,024-dimension vectors are stored as int8 for a rescoring layer. How much RAM does that take?
quiz.explanation: int8 is one byte per dimension: 10 million × 1,024 B ≈ 10.2 GB.

quiz.question: A news archive’s end-to-end recall is 0.80, while each later layer keeps almost everything it receives. What fixes it?
options: Keeping more candidates in the first layer
quiz.explanation: Later layers cannot recover what layer 1 dropped, so layer 1 needs a larger candidate set.

quiz.question: A Qdrant query asks for limit = 100 with oversampling = 4.0 and rescoring on. How many candidates are fetched from the quantized index?
quiz.explanation: Oversampling multiplies the limit: 100 × 4 = 400 candidates are rescored with full vectors to return 100.

quiz.question: Layer 1 costs 3 ms plus 0.004 ms per candidate and keeps 2,000. Layer 2 rescores those at 0.003 ms each and keeps 100. Layer 3 fetches the 100 at 0.05 ms each. A cross-encoder takes 1.2 ms per pair for 10 pairs. Total latency?
Which layer designs are reasonable for 50 million support chunks? Select all that apply.
options: Binary codes in RAM for layer 1
int8 rescoring of a few thousand candidates
Fetching full vectors from SSD only for the last hundred
Running the cross-encoder over all 50 million chunks
quiz.explanation: Each layer is sized to what it can afford. A cross-encoder over the whole corpus would take hours.

quiz.question: Why add an int8 layer between the binary scan and the float32 rescore? Select all that apply.
options: It avoids fetching thousands of float32 vectors from SSD
It restores most of the precision lost by binary codes
It recovers neighbours the binary layer dropped
quiz.explanation: int8 narrows the set cheaply and accurately in RAM. It can only reorder what layer 1 kept.

quiz.question: A cross-encoder costs 1.2 ms per pair and re-ranks 50 passages, pushing a 50 ms budget over. What is the most direct fix?
options: Re-rank fewer passages, such as 20, which takes 24 ms
quiz.explanation: 50 × 1.2 = 60 ms breaks the budget; 20 × 1.2 = 24 ms fits.

quiz.question: A vendor says its product does “layered approximate search”. What should you understand by that?
options: A pattern rather than one standard algorithm: products call it phased ranking or rescoring, so check what it does
quiz.explanation: The name means different things in different products. Ask which layers it runs and how many candidates each keeps.

quiz.question: Which product expresses layered ranking as first-phase, second-phase and global-phase?
quiz.explanation: Vespa’s phased ranking runs a cheap first phase over many hits and costlier phases over fewer.

quiz.question: Binary quantization replaces 32-bit floats with 1 bit per dimension. What is the compression factor?
quiz.explanation: 32 bits ÷ 1 bit = 32×.

quiz.question: Which measurements do you need to size each layer? Select all that apply.
options: Layer 1 recall at several candidate counts
quiz.explanation: Sizing is empirical: measure what each layer keeps and costs, and check the whole pipeline.

quiz.question: Layer 1 keeps 0.90 of the true top 10. Every later layer keeps everything and a cross-encoder orders the result. What is the best possible vector recall@10?
options: It depends only on the cross-encoder
quiz.explanation: Later layers only reorder what layer 1 kept, so recall is capped at 0.90.

quiz.question: How much RAM do binary codes need for 200 million 1,024-dimension vectors?
quiz.explanation: 1,024 bits = 128 B per vector, and 200 million × 128 B = 25.6 GB.

quiz.question: Which FAISS index rescores results from a quantized index with full vectors?
quiz.explanation: IndexRefineFlat wraps a compressed index and re-ranks its candidates with exact distances.

quiz.question: Which of these make the first layer miss true neighbours? Select all that apply.
options: Binary codes that lose too much information for this embedding model
quiz.explanation: A narrow or lossy first layer drops neighbours. The final re-ranker cannot cause first-layer misses.

quiz.question: Layer 1 keeps 0.98 of true neighbours at 1,000 candidates and 0.995 at 3,000, which adds 8 ms. The pipeline has 10 ms to spare. What do you choose?
quiz.explanation: The extra recall is permanent and fits the spare budget, since 8 ms is below 10 ms.

quiz.question: Where must full-precision vectors live for the final rescore?
options: Somewhere retrievable, such as on SSD; they need not be in RAM
quiz.explanation: Only the few final candidates need full vectors, so they can be fetched from disk.
